title: Classical and religious natural law
subtitle: Aquinas, Cicero and the claim that unjust law fails to bind
objectives: State the core natural law claim that human law is grounded in, and answerable to, a higher moral order rather than being self-validating
Set out Aquinas's four-fold scheme of law (eternal, natural, human, divine) and explain how human law is supposed to derive from natural law
Explain the doctrine lex injusta non est lex and what Aquinas actually says follows from it for a citizen's conscience

leadingAuthorities.role: The 'Treatise on Law' — the four-fold scheme of law and the conditions a human law must meet to be genuine law
The classical (pre-Christian) statement that true law is 'right reason in agreement with nature', binding independently of what any state enacts

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Natural law is the oldest position in this module, and the one most often caricatured in exam answers as 'law must be moral or it's not law, full stop'. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You can name Aquinas's four kinds of law — this lesson checks whether you can state precisely what he says follows, and doesn't follow, from an unjust statute.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below leans on precision: expect questions that test exactly what lex injusta non est lex does and doesn't claim, not just that you can recite the Latin.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and take it slowly — the four-fold scheme in Part 3 assumes you already have the basic natural law claim (law answerable to a higher moral order) clearly in mind.

overview.hook: In 1945, prosecutors at Nuremberg faced a hard question: the defendants had broken no law of the state that employed them, and had often followed it to the letter. Was that a defence? Centuries earlier, Aquinas had already argued that some rules only look like law — that a statute can fail to bind in conscience however properly it was enacted. This lesson starts where that argument starts: not with Nuremberg, but with Aquinas's own four-fold picture of what law is, and Cicero's older claim that true law was never simply whatever the state says it is.

parts.heading: The natural law claim, stated plainly
parts.voice: argumentative — states the position before any of its later complications
body: Natural law theory's central claim is easy to state and easy to misstate. Properly put: human-made law is grounded in, and answerable to, a higher moral order that exists independently of any legislature — and a rule that seriously violates that order is defective as law, not merely as morality.

This is a stronger claim than 'unjust laws are bad' or 'we should try to make good laws'. Almost every legal theory, including its rivals in this module, agrees with that much. What is distinctive about natural law is the further claim that morality is not simply an external standard for criticising law, but partly constitutive of what counts as law at all — so that a sufficiently unjust enactment is not just bad law, but arguably not really law in the fullest sense.

Two things to hold onto before this gets more technical. First, natural law long predates Christianity — Cicero was writing about a law grounded in nature and reason a century before Christ. Second, 'natural' here does not mean biological instinct; it means a moral order discoverable by reason (and, for the religious versions, ultimately grounded in God), which is why this lesson pairs a Roman statesman with a thirteenth-century Dominican friar without contradiction.

components.definition: The theory that human law is grounded in, and answerable to, a higher moral order — whether described as the law of nature, right reason, or divine law — such that a law seriously violating that order is defective as law, not merely as morality.

interaction.prompt: A student writes: 'Natural law theory just means believing that unjust laws are bad and should be changed.' Is that an accurate statement of the theory's distinctive claim?
options: No — natural law makes the stronger claim that a sufficiently unjust rule is defective as law itself, not merely bad policy
Yes — that is the whole of the natural law position
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Almost every theory in this module agrees that unjust laws are bad and should be changed. Natural law's distinctive move is treating morality as partly constitutive of legal validity itself.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: That statement is too weak — nearly every rival theory in this module would also agree that unjust laws are bad. Natural law's distinctive claim goes further: a seriously unjust rule is defective as law, not just as policy.

parts.heading: Cicero: true law before the Church
parts.voice: case-narrative — introduces the classical source before the religious one
body: Natural law's oldest surviving statement in Western legal thought comes not from a theologian but from a Roman statesman. In De Re Publica, written in the first century BC, Cicero describes 'true law' as right reason in agreement with nature: of universal application, unchanging, and the same at Rome as at Athens, now and in the future — a law that no senate or popular vote can repeal, because it was never made by any legislature in the first place.

Notice what this rules out. If true law is universal and unchanging, then a decree of the Roman Senate that contradicts it is not simply a competing law of equal standing — it is, on Cicero's account, something less than fully law, however formally valid within Rome's own institutions. This is the same move Aquinas will later formalise with more theological apparatus: an enacted rule is measured against a standard it did not create and cannot alter.

Cicero's version is explicitly secular in its reasoning, even though he assumes a divine author behind nature's order — reason, not revelation, is what lets a human being recognise the law of nature. That emphasis on reason as the route to natural law is the thread Aquinas picks up and develops into the four-fold scheme in the next part of this lesson.

components.citation: Cicero, De Re Publica, Book III (trans., commonly cited passage)
components.text: True law is right reason in agreement with nature; it is of universal application, unchanging and everlasting... It is a sin to try to alter this law, nor is it allowable to attempt to repeal any part of it, and it is impossible to abolish it entirely. We cannot be freed from its obligations by any decree of the senate or the people... there will not be one law at Rome and another at Athens, one now and another in the future, but one eternal and unchangeable law will be valid for all nations and all times.
elements: Universal application — not limited to one state or people
Unchanging — the same across time and place
Not created by, or repealable by, any legislature
Grounded in reason's agreement with nature, not in enactment

interaction.prompt: In Cicero's passage above, highlight the sentence that most directly denies that a legislature can alter true law.

parts.heading: Aquinas's four-fold scheme of law
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: Aquinas's Treatise on Law, in the Summa Theologiae (I-II, qq. 90–97), organises everything Cicero gestured at into a precise four-part structure. Getting the order and the relationships right matters more than memorising definitions in isolation, because each kind of law is defined by its relationship to the others.

Eternal law is God's rational plan governing the whole universe — the ultimate source from which everything else derives. Natural law is the rational creature's participation in eternal law: the portion of that plan a human being can grasp through reason alone, without revelation, summarised by Aquinas as the basic precept that good is to be done and pursued, and evil avoided. Human law (positive law, the law of states) is derived from natural law by human reason working out its practical implications for a particular community — Aquinas calls this process of derivation determinatio, and it is crucial for the next lesson on Finnis, who builds an entire modern theory around this one idea. Divine law is a fourth, separate category: truths revealed directly through scripture, given because natural reason alone cannot fully direct a human being toward their supernatural end.

The order matters: human law is meant to answer to natural law, and natural law is meant to answer to eternal law — not the reverse. A human statute doesn't create the standard it's judged against; it's supposed to derive from one.

components.label: Aquinas's four kinds of law
points: Eternal law — God's rational plan governing the whole universe; the ultimate source
Natural law — the rational creature's participation in eternal law, grasped through reason alone: 'good is to be done and pursued, and evil avoided'
Human (positive) law — derived from natural law by human reason applying it to a particular community's circumstances (determinatio)
Divine law — truths revealed through scripture, needed because reason alone cannot fully direct a person to their supernatural end

interaction.prompt: Put Aquinas's four kinds of law in the order of derivation he sets out — from the ultimate source to the most particular.
items: Eternal law (God's rational plan for the universe)
Natural law (the rational creature's grasp of eternal law through reason)
Human law (natural law applied to a particular community by determinatio)
Divine law (truths revealed through scripture, for a supernatural end)
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the scheme: eternal law is the source, natural law is what reason grasps of it, human law derives from natural law for a particular community, and divine law is a separate, revealed supplement rather than a further step in the same chain.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the derivation chain again — eternal law comes first as the ultimate source, natural law is reason's grasp of it, and human law derives from natural law by determinatio. Divine law is revealed separately, not a further step down the same chain.

parts.heading: Lex injusta non est lex: what Aquinas actually says
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the hard question before resolving it precisely
body: Here is the question every exam script on this topic eventually has to answer precisely, because most get it slightly wrong: does Aquinas say that an unjust law simply isn't law at all, full stop — so that it can be ignored like a stranger's opinion? Not quite.

Aquinas sets out conditions a human law must meet to count as genuine law: it must be an ordinance of reason, made for the common good, by one who has proper care of the community, and duly promulgated. A law failing these conditions — because it serves private advantage rather than the common good, or exceeds the lawmaker's authority, or is unjust in its content — is, in Aquinas's words, 'not law but a corruption of law', and 'has more the nature of violence than of law'.

But look carefully at what Aquinas draws from this. He does not say an unjust law can simply be ignored with no further thought. He distinguishes laws unjust because they conflict with human good (which do not bind in conscience, though he cautions that disobedience should still avoid scandal or greater disorder where possible) from laws that positively require something contrary to divine law (which not only fail to bind, but must not be obeyed at all, even at serious personal cost). The Latin tag lex injusta non est lex — 'an unjust law is not a law' — compresses a genuinely careful, graded position into a slogan that loses most of its nuance.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often write that Aquinas holds an unjust law simply has no legal existence at all, and that natural law theory therefore licenses ignoring any law you personally find unfair.
components.whyItsWrong: Aquinas's actual position is graded and conditional. A law can be unjust in the sense of failing the four conditions for genuine law (reason, common good, proper authority, promulgation) without collapsing entirely — he treats such laws as not binding in conscience, while still urging caution about open disobedience to avoid civil disorder, except where the law positively commands something contrary to divine law, which must be refused outright. This is a long way from 'ignore any law you find unfair'.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that Aquinas's lex injusta non est lex means a citizen may simply disregard any law they personally judge to be unjust?
sliderLabels: Confident — his actual position is far more conditional than that
interaction.correctPosition: Confident — his actual position is far more conditional than that
interaction.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes laws unjust for failing the four conditions of genuine law (which do not bind in conscience, but disobedience should still weigh the risk of scandal or disorder) from laws commanding something contrary to divine law (which must be refused outright, whatever the cost). Neither branch amounts to a general licence to disregard any law one personally dislikes.

parts.heading: What follows for a citizen's conscience — and what doesn't
parts.voice: reflective — closes the lesson by drawing out the practical stakes
body: Why does any of this matter to a modern lawyer rather than a theologian? Because the claim that an unjust 'law' fails to bind in conscience is doing real work wherever law and radical injustice have coexisted — colonial legal systems, apartheid-era statutes, and, most famously in this module's later material, the Nazi legal order that the Hart–Fuller debate confronts directly.

Natural law in this classical form gives a principled route to saying: a rule can be law in the sense that it was enacted through the correct institutional procedure, and enforced by courts and police, while still failing to be law in the fuller sense that matters for conscience — because it fails the substantive test of justice that Aquinas builds into the very definition of human law. That is a genuinely different move from simply saying 'this law is bad, and I refuse to follow it' as a matter of personal conviction; it is a claim about what law itself requires to count as law at all.

Keep the distinction sharp as you move to the next lesson. Finnis, writing eight centuries after Aquinas and largely without the theology, keeps this basic structure — human law measured against a higher standard grasped by reason — while reframing what that higher standard consists of and what, precisely, follows when human law falls short of it.

components.definition: 'An unjust law is not a law' — a compressed Latin summary of Aquinas's graded claim that a human law failing the conditions of genuine law (reason, common good, proper authority, promulgation) does not bind in conscience, and that a law commanding something contrary to divine law must be refused outright.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario that would most directly trigger Aquinas's strongest category — a law that must be refused outright, not merely one that fails to bind in conscience.
interaction.scenarioText: A regime enacts a tax rule that is procedurally valid but, in the assessor's view, serves the ruling faction's private enrichment rather than the common good. The same regime separately enacts a rule requiring citizens to actively participate in an act the assessor regards as gravely contrary to fundamental morality.
tappableSpans: serves the ruling faction's private enrichment
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. A rule that positively commands something gravely contrary to fundamental morality falls into Aquinas's strongest category — one that must be refused outright, not merely one that fails to bind in conscience while caution about disorder is weighed.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The tax rule serving private enrichment is Aquinas's weaker category — it fails to bind in conscience, but disobedience must still weigh scandal and disorder. Look instead for the rule that positively commands participation in something gravely immoral — that triggers his strongest category, an outright duty to refuse.

testPool.prompt: State natural law theory's central claim about the relationship between law and morality.
acceptableAnswers: law is grounded in and answerable to a higher moral order; unjust law is defective as law
human law derives from a higher moral order and a seriously unjust rule is defective as law, not just as morality
testPool.modelAnswer: Human law is grounded in, and answerable to, a higher moral order existing independently of any legislature. A rule that seriously violates that order is defective as law itself, not merely as policy or morality.

testPool.prompt: Name Aquinas's four kinds of law, in order of derivation.
acceptableAnswers: eternal law, natural law, human law, divine law
testPool.modelAnswer: Eternal law, natural law, human (positive) law, and divine law.

testPool.prompt: Which classical Roman source predates Aquinas in stating that 'true law' is grounded in reason and nature, not enactment?
According to Aquinas, which of the following is NOT one of the four conditions a human law must meet to count as genuine law?
options: Made by one with proper care of the community
testPool.trapExplanation: Aquinas's four conditions are: an ordinance of reason, made for the common good, by one who has care of the community, and duly promulgated. Unanimous popular approval is not one of his conditions — his framework is compatible with law made by a properly constituted authority that is not democratically elected.

testPool.prompt: Which statement most accurately captures what Aquinas says follows from lex injusta non est lex?
options: Any law a citizen personally believes is unjust may simply be disregarded

A law failing the four conditions of genuine law does not bind in conscience, though disobedience should weigh scandal and disorder; a law commanding something contrary to divine law must be refused outright
Unjust laws remain fully binding until formally repealed by the state
testPool.trapExplanation: The first option flattens Aquinas's graded position into a general licence he never grants — his account is conditional and distinguishes degrees of injustice. The third option ignores the doctrine's whole point, which is precisely that some laws fail to bind despite formal validity.

testPool.prompt: In the passage below, highlight the sentence that states the condition a human law must meet to serve the common good, rather than private advantage.
testPool.passage: A human law is an ordinance of reason for the common good, made by one who has care of the community, and promulgated. Where a ruler enacts a rule chiefly to enrich themselves or their faction rather than to serve the community as a whole, that rule fails this condition, whatever else it formally satisfies. Such a law, Aquinas holds, is 'not law but a corruption of law'.
testPool.ratioSentence: Where a ruler enacts a rule chiefly to enrich themselves or their faction rather than to serve the community as a whole, that rule fails this condition, whatever else it formally satisfies.

testPool.prompt: Order these steps in Aquinas's reasoning about whether a human law binds in conscience.
items: Check whether the law is an ordinance of reason, for the common good, by a proper authority, duly promulgated
If any condition fails, classify the law as unjust rather than genuine law
Ask whether the law merely fails to serve the common good, or positively commands something contrary to divine law
Apply the corresponding conclusion: no binding in conscience (with caution about disorder), or an outright duty to refuse

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that Cicero's account of 'true law' in De Re Publica is grounded in Christian revelation?
sliderLabels: Confident — it is a Christian doctrine
Confident — it predates and is independent of Christian revelation
testPool.correctPosition: Confident — it predates and is independent of Christian revelation
testPool.explanation: Cicero was writing in the first century BC, roughly a century before Christ, and grounds true law in reason's agreement with nature rather than in scripture. Natural law's religious versions, including Aquinas's, come later and build on this classical foundation rather than originating it.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario that shows the rule fails Aquinas's 'common good' condition for genuine law.
testPool.scenarioText: A city council, acting entirely within its formal legal powers and following the correct procedure, passes a bylaw redirecting public funds earmarked for road repairs into the personal accounts of three councillors, with no benefit to residents at all.
tappableSpans: acting entirely within its formal legal powers
into the personal accounts of three councillors
no benefit to residents at all
testPool.correctSpan: no benefit to residents at all
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Right. Formal validity (correct powers, correct procedure) is not in question here — what fails Aquinas's test is that the rule serves private enrichment with no benefit to the community, breaching the common-good condition regardless of how properly it was enacted.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Procedural correctness is a distraction here — Aquinas's common-good condition looks past that to whether the rule actually serves the community. Look for the fact showing residents get nothing from it at all.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario best illustrates Aquinas's strongest category — a law that must be refused outright, not merely one that fails to bind in conscience?
testPool.scenarioA: A tax statute, properly enacted, that funds a project widely regarded as wasteful but not otherwise harmful
testPool.scenarioB: A statute requiring officials to actively participate in the torture of prisoners as a matter of policy
testPool.explanation: B commands active participation in something gravely contrary to fundamental morality — Aquinas's strongest category, which must be refused outright. A is, at most, a candidate for his weaker category (failing the common-good test, so not binding in conscience) but involves no positive command to do something gravely immoral.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following claims is closer to Cicero's position than to a purely descriptive account of law?
testPool.scenarioA: 'Whatever the Roman Senate enacts through the correct procedure counts as law at Rome, whether or not it is just.'
testPool.scenarioB: 'True law exists independently of any senate's enactment, and no decree can free a person from its obligations.'
testPool.explanation: B mirrors Cicero directly: true law is prior to, and independent of, any legislative act, and cannot be repealed by one. A instead states a purely descriptive, institution-based account of validity that Cicero's classical natural law position is arguing against.

testPool.prompt: In the extract below, which phrase does the most work in denying that human law is self-validating — that it creates the standard it is judged against?
options: 'human law is derived from natural law by human reason applying it to a particular community's circumstances'
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The word 'derived' is doing the key work — it marks human law as dependent on, and answerable to, a prior standard (natural law), rather than as the ultimate source of legal validity in its own right.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Focus on the phrase that expresses dependency — human law being derived from something prior, rather than standing on its own as the ultimate source of validity.

testPool.prompt: A legislature, acting through its normal constitutional procedure, passes a statute stripping a minority group of the right to own property, purely on the basis of group membership. On Aquinas's four conditions, which is most clearly violated?
options: Promulgation — the law was not properly published
The common good — the law serves no end but the domination of one group by another, at odds with the community's genuine good
Proper authority — the legislature lacked the constitutional power to pass any statute
testPool.explanation: The scenario stipulates correct procedure and proper authority, and says nothing to suggest a promulgation defect — so those conditions are, on the facts given, satisfied. What fails is the common-good condition: a rule built on group domination cannot be an ordinance directed at the genuine common good of the community as a whole.

testPool.prompt: A civil servant is ordered, under a properly enacted regulation, to withhold food aid from a famine-affected region as a matter of settled government policy, with no security or logistical justification offered. Using Aquinas's framework, analyse whether the civil servant is bound in conscience to comply.
factsToOrder: The regulation was properly enacted through the correct constitutional procedure
The regulation serves no security or logistical purpose
Compliance would require actively causing serious harm (withholding food aid) to people in need
No countervailing justification for the harm is offered

scaffolds.support: Full model answer shown, mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes the Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes the Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes the full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the civil servant is bound in conscience to comply with a properly enacted regulation that requires actively causing serious harm with no justification.
modelAnswer.rule: Aquinas holds that a human law failing the common-good condition does not bind in conscience, though disobedience should weigh scandal and disorder; a law that positively commands something gravely contrary to fundamental morality must be refused outright, regardless of the cost.
modelAnswer.application: Formal enactment through the correct procedure is not in dispute, but that alone does not settle the matter on Aquinas's account. The regulation both fails the common-good condition (it serves no genuine end for the community, only harm with no offsetting justification) and, more significantly, positively commands active participation in serious harm to people in need — the stronger category Aquinas treats as requiring outright refusal.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The civil servant is not bound in conscience to comply, and on Aquinas's account is under a positive duty to refuse, whatever the personal cost of doing so.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The single most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating lex injusta non est lex as a blunt licence to disregard any law one dislikes. Aquinas's actual position is graded: failing the common-good test means a law does not bind in conscience, but caution about disorder still applies — only a law commanding something gravely contrary to divine law must be refused outright.
